messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
David is a 67-year-old married man who has spent most of his adult life working in hotels and now manages a midrange property near a busy highway interchange. He describes himself as someone who used to be steady with people, the kind of manager who could calm an angry guest, joke with the night clerk, and walk the property late in the evening without much thought. That changed after he was robbed several months ago while leaving the hotel after a late shift.

It had been a routine night by his standards. A wedding reception had run long, and there had been spilled drinks in the ballroom and several intoxicated guests lingering in the parking lot. David stayed behind to help close out the day, then stepped outside through the employee entrance carrying paperwork and his wallet in his jacket pocket. The air near the back lot still carried the stale, sour smell of alcohol from the reception, and he noticed two men standing near the edge of the lot. He remembers registering them as off somehow, hanging back rather than heading to their cars, watching instead of moving. Before he could turn away, one of them came toward him fast. There was shouting, a demand for his wallet, a shove hard enough to throw him off balance, and then another blow when he hesitated. A car door slammed somewhere nearby, and one of the men yelled again. David recalls the shock less as a sequence than as a felt certainty that he was trapped with men he could not read and could not stop. What stayed with him most was the combination of the alcohol on their breath, the sharp burst of noise in the lot, and the realization that being experienced, older, and in charge had not protected him at all.

In the days that followed, he returned to work because he felt he had to, but the hotel no longer felt like familiar ground. He found himself scanning the lobby, the bar area, and the parking lot for anyone who looked suspicious to him: people lingering too long by entrances, guests who kept their hands in their pockets, men standing in pairs and watching the desk. He knew other people might see ordinary hotel traffic, but he had come to believe the world was plainly dangerous and that assuming otherwise was how a man got blindsided. When someone approached him unexpectedly from behind in a hallway or placed a hand on his shoulder to get his attention, he reacted with alarm before he could think, jerking away or spinning around, embarrassed immediately afterward. Loud noises inside the hotel—the bang of a service door, a dropped tray from the restaurant, a sudden shout from the bar—hit him in the body like a fresh warning.

The smell of alcohol became especially difficult. Because the hotel hosted receptions and served drinks in the lounge, he encountered it often: on carpets after an event, on guests crowding the elevators, on a businessman leaning across the front desk late at night. Each time, David felt himself tighten and watch more closely. He began changing his routines in small ways that built up over time. He avoided walking the back lot alone, delegated more evening issues to assistant managers, and lingered in the office rather than circulating through the property as he once had. Staff noticed he was less approachable and more abrupt when he questioned them about unfamiliar people on the premises. At home, his wife expected that he would finally relax, but he did not. He checked locks repeatedly, listened for sounds outside, and stayed on guard even in his own living room. If she touched him unexpectedly while passing behind his chair, he startled so sharply that both of them were shaken.

What troubled David nearly as much as the fear was the humiliation. He had spent a lifetime seeing himself as competent and hard to rattle. Now he felt permanently diminished by the fact that he had been overpowered in the parking lot of his own hotel. He was certain that people could not be trusted, and this conviction spread beyond the men who robbed him. Guests, strangers in line at the gas station, even people walking too slowly past his house all drew his suspicion. He did not describe this as cynicism; to him it felt like realism, the only sane response to what he had learned.

He finally agreed to seek help after an incident at work when a banquet server tapped him unexpectedly during a noisy event and he wheeled around so aggressively that he frightened the young man and drew the attention of nearby guests. His wife had already been urging him to talk to someone, telling him that he was no longer at ease anywhere, not even at home. David comes to treatment ashamed of how much of his life now feels organized around watchfulness, but also convinced that letting his guard down would be reckless. What frightens him most is the idea that this wary, humiliated version of himself is now permanent. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to move through the hotel and his own house without feeling that danger is waiting just outside his line of sight.
